newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU leaders struggle into night over treaty.
newsitem.headline: EU leaders struggle into night over treaty.

text.p: European Union leaders struggled into the night on Tuesday to set the balance of power in the 15-nation bloc ahead of a planned expansion into eastern Europe.

Two days of horse-trading that have seen national sensitivities derail a number of agreements sought by keen European integrationists came down to a difficult session between large and small EU countries over their clout.
The fight centred on the demand by the bloc's large countries that they recoup some of the power in decision-making that they have lost through the arrival of newcomers such as Sweden and Finland.

Although small countries are insistent on not being overrun, the issue is considered crucial by the bloc's powers as the EU plans to bring in as many as a dozen new and relatively small members from eastern Europe.

The Dutch EU presidency began the discussion by pointing out that the bloc's five largest countries would be asked to give up one of their European commissioners within a few years and needed more power in ministerial meeting to make up for it.

French President Jacques Chirac and Spanish Prime Minister Jose-Maria Aznar dismissed a proposal to create a two-tier decision-making system -- involving consideration of population -- as a new confusion in an already arcane system.
Most progress on Tuesday came by diluting earlier proposals.
Britain, Ireland and Denmark were given opt-outs from parts of the treaty in a move that leaders hoped would prompt closer cooperation in crime fighting and immigration policy.

London and Dublin would retain their borders and the right to set their own visa, immigration and asylum policy. Copenhagen's opt-out reflects constitutional problems with passing sovereignty to EU institutions.
France settled for the appointment of a senior, but relatively obscure, Eurocrat to take on the task of coordinating EU foreign policy, deferring for now on its desire for a high-profile candidate.
National sensitivities, meanwhile, ensured that the veto would remain in areas of immigration and refugee policy while Germany made sure its was extended to asylum policy, too.
The move was a blow to those who have argued over the 15 months of talks that majority voting is necessary for the bloc to be effective.

Under the latest draft treaty, EU countries would agree to cooperate more closely in areas such as asylum, immigration, visa policy and crime fighting. Breaking from current practice, the European Commission would be allowed to recommend rules.
The Schengen accord, linking most of the bloc's members in a partially completed border-free zone, would also be incorporated into the EU, lifting frontiers throughout the continent.
Britain, Ireland and Denmark would be given various opt-outs to meet their internal political concerns.

British Prime Minister Tony Blair, as unbending in some areas as his predecessors if not as strident, vetoed plans to bring the Western European Union (WEU) into the EU over time, leaving the treaty's text on defence saying simply that incorporation was a possibility.
With one eye on the citizens they are seeking to court, the leaders have also agreed that an Employment Chapter should be put into the treaty to raise job creation high in the agenda.
